newsitem.title: UK: IRA still "well-stocked for war" - British source.
newsitem.headline: IRA still "well-stocked for war" - British source.

text.p: A major arms and explosives haul in Britain on Monday was a security and publicity coup against the outlawed IRA but the Irish guerrillas still have enough arms to wage war into the next century, security sources said.

"They have enough assault rifles to arm two battalions," a British official said about arms dumps hidden in the Irish Republic that have fuelled a long war to drive British forces out of Northern Ireland.

Crucially, British intelligence officers say the Irish Republican Army (IRA) also has sufficient quantities of plastic explosives to continue targeting high profile "economic targets" and bring mayhem to mainland Britain for years.

A suspect was killed on Monday during the police raids said to have foiled an imminent IRA bomb attack in Britain. Police said they had recovered a "very large" quantity of explosives as well as firearms and bomb-making equipment.
The raids confuse further an already complex picture about whether the IRA is ready to renew an 17-month ceasefire broken in February by a series of bombs in London.

The big question puzzling London and Dublin -- joint sponsors of a drive to create a new peace climate in Northern Ireland -- is whether the guerrillas have the will to take their fight against British rule into the new millennium.

Irish Prime Minister John Bruton triggered new optimism about the peace process on a trip two weeks ago to the United States, suggesting a new truce might be at hand. British and Irish media, quoting security sources, backed his assessment.

Press reports said it could be preceded by a final "big bang" by the IRA just to prove to London that it was operating from a position of strength. Republicans moved quickly to douse the speculation, saying the reports were groundless.
Hardline republicans say the absence of guerrilla attacks in Northern Ireland since February is a message to London that they do not want to push the province over the brink.
Some independent analysts say they do not believe conditions yet exist for an imminent peace breakthrough.
But they detect signs that a new effort is under way to test the water, possibly in background contacts that have gone on for years between the Republicans and their British enemies.
British security sources say Monday's deadly cache proves that the guerrillas remain on a war footing and were preparing to end a four-month lull in a bombing campaign.
"Their stockpiles could arm a small army," a security source said.

Intelligence experts say the underground army has hundreds of AK 47 assault rifles, at least 20 armour-piercing machine guns, as well as general purpose machine guns, piles of rocket launchers and a few surface-to-air missiles.
Many of the weapons were smuggled from Libya during a war that started in 1969 and has claimed more than 3,200 lives.
The IRA has also used home-grown engineering expertise to make its own lethal weapons, including huge "barrack buster" mortars that have wrecked police stations.

IRA attacks have put enormous strains on a two-year truce by their arch-foes in pro-British Protestant extremists groups, with some Protestant hardmen urging a backlash against the Irish capital Dublin or random Catholics nationalists.
Britain says the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, will not be given a seat in multi-party political talks while the IRA wages war.

Republicans say Britain went back on a promise of a seat at the talks for Sinn Fein after the IRA's first truce and the guerrillas want solid guarantees of talks on a united Ireland before calling another ceasefire.
